events.title: The accession of Diocletian
events.shortBlurb: On a hill outside Nicomedia the army hailed a Dalmatian officer as Augustus, and the Church of Egypt would one day date its Era of Martyrs from his reign…
body: After the deaths of the emperor Carus and his son Numerian, the army of the East gathered on 20 November 284 on a hill some miles outside Nicomedia in Bithynia. There the officers saluted the commander of the household troops, Diocles, as their new Augustus; he accepted the purple, swore he had no part in Numerian's death, and soon Latinized his name to Diocletianus. He was to reign twenty-one years and then, alone among Roman emperors, to abdicate.

Diocletian restored order after the long anarchy of the third century, reorganizing the empire under the fourfold rule of the Tetrarchy. Yet in 303 he unleashed the Great Persecution, the last and most systematic assault the pagan state ever made upon the Christians, with edicts to destroy the churches, burn the Scriptures, and compel sacrifice.

So many were the martyrs of those years that the Church of Alexandria reckoned its calendar as the "Era of Martyrs" (Anno Martyrum), counting from his accession — a reckoning the Coptic Church keeps to this day. Lactantius, in his account of the deaths of the persecutors, preserves the day of his proclamation.

sources.text: Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors (public-domain translation)
